title: How to Use MLS Data to Analyze Investment Properties Like a Pro
excerpt: MLS data is one of the most powerful tools available to real estate investors, but most people only scratch the surface of what it can reveal. Learn how to dig deeper into comps, days on market, price trends, and more to find your next profitable deal.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to use MLS data to analyze investment properties
metaDescription: Learn how to use MLS data to analyze investment properties with this step-by-step guide covering comps, market trends, and key metrics for investors.
metaKeywords: how to use MLS data to analyze investment properties, MLS data for investors, real estate comps, investment property analysis, MLS market trends, days on market, real estate data analysis, property investment research

sections.content: The Multiple Listing Service — better known as the MLS — holds a goldmine of information that most investors barely tap into. Sure, everyone uses it to browse listings. But the investors who consistently find profitable deals use MLS data in a much smarter way. They analyze trends, track market velocity, and build comp models before they ever make an offer. If you want to sharpen your analysis game, this guide walks you through exactly how to use MLS data to analyze investment properties from the ground up. For a broader framework on evaluating markets, check out this [Real Estate Market Analysis for Investors: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-market-analysis) before diving in.
What Is MLS Data and Why Does It Matter for Investors?

The MLS is a shared database that real estate agents use to list and search properties. It contains detailed records for active listings, pending sales, and sold properties — sometimes going back years. For investors, the sold data is where the real value lives. Every closed sale tells you what a buyer actually paid, not just what a seller hoped for. That distinction matters enormously when you are trying to estimate after-repair value (ARV), project rental income, or determine whether a market is heating up or cooling off.

Access to the MLS typically requires a real estate license or a relationship with a licensed agent. Some investors partner with investor-friendly agents specifically to get MLS access. Others use platforms that aggregate MLS data through licensed feeds. Either way, having reliable, up-to-date sold data is non-negotiable if you want to make confident offers. Learn more about structuring your research workflow in our guide on [How to Use MLS Data for Investment Research](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/mls-data-real-estate-investors).
Step 1: Pull Comparable Sales (Comps) the Right Way

The foundation of any investment property analysis is a solid set of comps. A comp, short for comparable sale, is a recently sold property that closely matches the one you are evaluating. Most investors get this step wrong by casting too wide a net or using outdated data. Here is how to do it right.

items: Radius: Start within 0.5 miles of the subject property. Expand to 1 mile only if you cannot find enough sales.
Time frame: Use sales from the last 90 days. In slower markets, you may need to stretch to 6 months, but always note when you do.
Property type: Match the type exactly — single-family to single-family, condo to condo. Do not mix property types.
Square footage: Stay within 20% of the subject property's size. A 1,000 sq ft home and a 1,800 sq ft home are not comparable.
Condition and updates: Look for properties with a similar level of finish. A fully renovated comp will inflate your ARV if the subject needs work.
Bedroom and bathroom count: A 3-bed/2-bath comp is the gold standard match for a 3-bed/2-bath subject.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Pull at least 5 to 8 comps and then remove the highest and lowest outliers before calculating your average price per square foot. This gives you a cleaner, more defensible ARV estimate. You can also run your numbers quickly using our free [Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to see if a deal pencils out.
Step 2: Track Days on Market to Gauge Demand

Days on market (DOM) is one of the most telling metrics in MLS data, and most beginners ignore it completely. DOM measures how long a property sat on the market before going under contract. In a hot market, homes might go pending in 7 to 14 days. In a soft market, that number might stretch to 60, 90, or even 120 days. For investors, a low average DOM means you can flip faster and hold carrying costs down. A high DOM signals that buyers have leverage, which affects your exit strategy.

When analyzing a specific neighborhood, look at the average DOM for all sold properties over the last 6 months, not just the ones that match your subject property. If the market-wide average is 18 days but the specific micro-neighborhood you are targeting shows a 55-day average, that is a red flag worth investigating before you commit capital. Tracking metrics like these consistently is a habit that separates disciplined investors from those who get burned. See our article on [Real Estate Market Indicators Every Investor Should Track](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/real-estate-market-indicators) for the full list of numbers worth watching.
Step 3: Analyze List-to-Sale Price Ratios

The list-to-sale price ratio tells you how close to asking price properties are actually selling. A ratio of 100% means homes are selling at exactly their list price. Ratios above 100% indicate bidding wars. Ratios below 95% suggest buyers are negotiating sellers down, which usually means the market has more supply than demand. For investors, this metric directly informs your offer strategy. In a market with a 98% average list-to-sale ratio, offering 85 cents on the dollar is probably a waste of everyone's time. In a market sitting at 91%, you have real room to negotiate.
Reading the Numbers in Real Markets

Take three different markets as examples. In a competitive market like [Seattle, WA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/seattle-wa), list-to-sale ratios have historically run above 100% in desirable zip codes, meaning investors need to be precise with their ARV calculations and move fast. In [Denver, CO](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/denver-co), ratios have moderated in recent years as inventory increased, creating more room to negotiate on distressed properties. In [Miami, FL](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/miami-fl), condo and single-family dynamics differ dramatically by neighborhood, so you have to drill down to the zip code level rather than relying on city-wide averages.
Step 4: Identify Price Per Square Foot Trends Over Time

Beyond individual comps, look at how price per square foot has trended over the past 12 to 24 months in your target area. If the median price per square foot has moved from $145 to $172 over two years, that is an 18.6% appreciation rate — well above average and worth noting for your hold vs. flip decision. Conversely, if price per square foot has been flat or declining, you need to bake lower appreciation assumptions into your projections.

"The best investors don't just look at what a property is worth today. They look at where the market is going and whether the numbers still work if appreciation stalls for 12 months." — Common wisdom among experienced flippers and buy-and-hold investors alike.

Spotting a neighborhood that is peaking versus one that still has room to run is a critical skill. Markets that show rapidly accelerating price per square foot growth paired with shrinking inventory and low DOM may be approaching a ceiling. For a deeper look at reading those warning signs, our article on [How to Spot a Real Estate Bubble Before It Pops](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/how-to-spot-real-estate-bubble) walks through the specific indicators to watch.
Step 5: Use Expired and Withdrawn Listings to Set Ceilings

Expired listings — properties that were listed but never sold — are just as valuable as sold comps. They tell you where the market ceiling is. If five homes in a neighborhood listed between $325,000 and $340,000 and none of them sold, that is a clear signal that buyers are not willing to pay those prices. When you are estimating ARV for a flip, expired listings help you avoid overestimating your exit price. Build your ARV from sold comps, then cross-check it against expireds to make sure you are not pricing yourself above what the market will bear.

This kind of layered analysis takes more time upfront, but it dramatically reduces the risk of a deal going sideways at exit. For a complete walkthrough of the full deal analysis process, including how to calculate repair costs, holding expenses, and profit margins, see our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals). And if you are building a portfolio rather than flipping, our [Passive Real Estate Investing](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/passive-real-estate-investing) guide covers how to apply similar analysis for long-term rental strategies.
Putting It All Together: A Simple MLS Analysis Checklist

items: Pull 5 to 8 sold comps within 0.5 miles, sold in the last 90 days, matching property type and size
Calculate average price per square foot and use it to estimate ARV
Check average DOM for the neighborhood — under 30 days is strong, over 60 is a caution sign
Review the list-to-sale ratio to calibrate your offer strategy
Track price per square foot trends over the last 12 to 24 months
Pull expired and withdrawn listings to identify the market ceiling
Run your deal numbers through a calculator to confirm your margin before making an offer
